title: My own size
hook: take a role beyond your powers and you fail it and neglect the one you could have filled (Enchiridion 37)
carry: the part that really was yours

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was banquet, and the biggest portion that loses its value at a shared table. Your line was for the sake of the fellowship.

The email says: we were hoping you'd chair the committee. You're flattered. You're also already behind on everything, you've never run a budget, and the committee meets on the night you usually put your kids to bed. You say yes anyway. Six months later the committee is struggling, and so is bedtime. Section thirty-seven of the handbook is a single sentence, and it names both things that went wrong.
screen: `WE HOPED YOU'D CHAIR THE COMMITTEE.` → `YOU SAY YES ANYWAY.` → `MY OWN SIZE.`

segments.voice: If you take on a role beyond your powers, Epictetus says, you disgrace yourself in it, and you neglect the role you could have filled. Two losses, not one. The Greek for role is prosōpon. It meant a face, then an actor's mask, then the part the mask stood for. Back in section seventeen you met this picture: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote, and your job is to play your part well. Today adds the other side: don't grab a part that isn't yours. Latin used persona for the same idea, mask and role together, and Cicero, drawing on an earlier Stoic, built a whole theory of the roles each person plays. Now the double cost. The first loss is obvious: the role you weren't ready for goes badly, and people see it. The second is quieter and usually bigger. The part that really was yours, the friend, the parent, the craftsman, the neighbor, gets the leftovers. Nobody throws a party for a role you neglected. It just thins out. What this isn't: a rule to stay small forever. In a couple of weeks the handbook will ask, sharply, how long you're going to wait to become your best. Growth is welcome. The point is honesty about your present size: what you can carry now, what you're for right now, and which yes would cost a part you've already been given.
screen: `A ROLE BEYOND YOUR POWERS.` · `PROSŌPON: FACE, MASK, ROLE.` · `TWO LOSSES: THAT ROLE, AND YOURS.` · `HONEST ABOUT YOUR PRESENT SIZE.` · then, large: `MY OWN SIZE.`

segments.voice: Think of what you've said yes to lately, the invitations, the asks, the jobs you took because nobody else would, and find one that's beyond your powers right now, or keeps eating time from a part that's really yours. Don't solve it; just name it. Then picture saying, kindly and clearly, I'm not the right person for this, and notice what loosens.
Prosōpon. The Greek word for mask, then role; take one beyond your powers and you fail it, and neglect the one you could have filled. Today's word.
Your line: the part that really was yours. Every yes spends a little of it. Day three hundred seventy-two, done.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review their commitments and decline roles beyond their present powers, to protect the roles they already hold.

notes: Enchiridion 37 paraphrased: if you assume a character beyond your powers, you both disgrace yourself in it and neglect the one you could have filled. Confirm.
Greek πρόσωπον in Ench. 37, and the sense progression face > mask > role: confirm.

'Cicero, drawing on an earlier Stoic, built a whole theory of roles' alludes to Panaetius' roles as presented in Cicero, De Officiis 1.107ff (personae). No etymology of persona is claimed. Confirm phrasing.

Audit (10% sample): the hook said Enchiridion 37 is 'two sentences long'; in the Greek and in Long 1877 it is one sentence. Changed to 'a single sentence'. Confirm against the edition a Keeper prefers.
